newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends US lower on Rubin, pre-payrolls squaring.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends US lower on Rubin, pre-payrolls squaring.

text.p: The dollar ended lower after a rally to a new 34-month high versus the mark fizzled as the market squared up before U.S. non-farm payrolls data on Friday, traders said.
In addition, dollar/yen came under pressure after comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin suggested that trade frictions with Japan were percolating.
"There is some reluctance to get involved ahead of (the February U.S. employment data) tomorrow," said Alfonso Alejo, corporate foreign exchange manager at Sakura Bank Ltd.
"There was a little more forcefulness in (selling) the dollar against yen just because of Rubin's commment having more bearing," Alejo added.
The dollar ended at 1.7160/70 marks, down from 1.7184/89 at the open. It fetched 121.08/18 yen, down from 121.58/68.
On Thursday, Rubin told reporters in Washington that a sustained current account surplus by Japan was in "nobody's interest."
The Treasury chief's remark came on the heels of a report from Japan showing the surplus in its current account surged in the year to January, its first increase in 17 months.

The dollar tends to fall when Japan's surplus swells since traders fear the Clinton administration may try to reverse the dollar's recent rally, believing it has made U.S. exports too expensive and given Japan a trade advantage.

The dollar jumped to 1.7210 marks in early U.S. trade after Germany released a report showing the adjusted number of jobless rose 5,000, while the unemployment rate was stuck at a stubbornly high 12.2 percent in February.
It got an extra boost after new claims for U.S. jobless benefits fell to 310,000 last week from 316,000 the previous week and factory orders jumped 2.5 percent in January.

"The point is there is probably a very small likelihood that German rates are going to go up but ... U.S. rates will have a tendency to go up," said Diego Giurleo, a treasury vice president at Royal Bank of Canada in New York.
"Fundamentally speaking, you have growth on the dollar side and you have strong interest rate differentials," he added.

Odds on a Federal Reserve interest rate hike at some point this year seemed to increase in recent days after Chairman Alan Greenspan told the U.S. Congress a credit tightening might be needed to prevent inflation from creeping up.
U.S. non-farm payrolls, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Friday, are expected to have increased 230,000 in February after a 271,000 rise in the previous month.
The unemployment rate, is forecast to have fallen to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent.

Traders also said the dollar received some support after the head of Germany's powerful machine plant and construction industry organization said on Thursday it would be appropriate for the dollar to strengthen to 1.80 to 2.0 against the mark.

"It makes sense for them to lobby for a weaker mark. If you are going to take their jobs away and you are going to cut back on their benefits, they have to look for some way to stay competitive, to at least keep their jobs," said John Barlow, senior dealer at Bayerische Landesbank Girozentrale.
Traders said rumors of European central bank offers above 1.72 marks also weighed in to cap the dollar's rise.

Elsewhere, the dollar was at 1.4815/25 Swiss francs, down from 1.4880/90 at the open. It fell to Canadian $1.3646/51 from C$1.3670/75. The pound rose to $1.6145/55 from $1.6108/18 and the Australian dollar rose to $0.7863/68 from $0.7862/67.
((--Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667))
